title: Kalmar Ottawa electric yard truck gets to work in Canada
content:
| Jul 26 2026 - 6:57 am PT
Kalmar Ottawa has been a leader in diesel-powered yard trucks for decades, but as global logistics fleets move to reduce costs and insulate themselves from volatile diesel prices, the company is making that shift, too – and they’re out to prove their new, battery-electric T2 EV can deliver the same durability and productivity that’s made the original T2 a fixture at ports for years.
With support from Transport Canada’s incentives for Medium- and Heavy-Duty Zero-Emission Vehicles
(“iMHZEV”) grant program, Canadian logistics firm WTC Group is putting a number of Kalmar Ottawa T2 EVs to work.
Innovation has always been central to WTC Group’s operations
,” explains Brad Gordon, Director of Maintenance at WTC. “As customers’ demand for sustainable logistics solutions continues to grow, investing in electric terminal tractors is a natural step in improving both operational efficiency and environmental performance.”
Kalmar is confident that its electric T2 will be up to whatever challenges WTC throws at it – and they should have a pretty good idea of what those are, having invented the specialized terminal tractor concept in 1943.
The Kalmar T2 EV itself is powered by a continuous-duty electric drive motor that can deliver up to 454 kW (~610 hp) at its peak output, drawing power from a modular li-ion battery pack available in 105, 140, or 210 kWh capacities, and can be spec’ed out to offer an almost inconceivable 195,000 lbs. GCWR (!). More than enough, in other words, choice to meet the needs of any of Kalmar’s customer fleets.
“Kalmar Ottawa has spent years developing the T2 EV to ensure (that) when we came to the market with an EV yard spotter, we would have the best EV truck in the market to match the reputation Kalmar established with our legendary T2 diesel terminal tractor that our customers have come to recognize,” said James Leibold,
Zero Emissions Vehicle Sales Manager
No word on how much WTC got from iMHZEV, or how many T2 EVs they’re deploying as part of the program.

title: Met police break their own record for seizing illegal e-bikes
content:
| Jul 26 2026 - 4:00 am PT
London’s Metropolitan Police have already confiscated more illegal e-bikes and e-scooters in 2026 than during the entirety of last year, as authorities continue an aggressive enforcement campaign targeting illegally modified micromobility vehicles.
reports that officers have seized more than 2,500 illegal e-bikes and e-scooters in just the first half of this year, surpassing the 2,241 vehicles confiscated throughout all of 2025. The effort is aimed at improving road safety while also reducing crimes such as phone thefts and robberies that police say are frequently committed using illegally modified two-wheelers.
In the UK, privately owned e-scooters that are popular in cities around the world remain illegal to ride on public roads, while legal e-bikes must comply with regulations limiting motor assistance to 15.5 mph (25 km/h) and meet other technical requirements.
According to the BBC, London’s Metropolitan Police have increasingly relied on
portable roadside dynamometers
, or “rolling roads,” to determine whether an e-bike has been illegally modified to exceed the legal speed limit. The Met is one of only two police forces in the UK currently deploying the portable testing equipment.
Police say common signs that prompt an inspection include unusually high speeds, oversized battery packs, and throttles capable of propelling a bike at speed without pedaling.
During one recent enforcement operation near Tottenham Court Road Station, officers reportedly seized 29 e-bikes and seven e-scooters in a single day. That operation was the seventh conducted this year, with another five planned throughout the summer.
Police believe the crackdown is contributing to lower crime rates, citing figures including that neighborhood offenses across London are down 14% over the past year, with a 23% reduction in theft from the person and an 11% decline in general robberies.
Commander Neerav Patel, who leads the Met’s e-bike enforcement efforts, told the BBC that while many people use e-bikes legitimately, police remain focused on those using illegally modified machines for criminal and anti-social behavior, particularly in connection with phone snatching incidents.

title: Exploring how CEOs Manage Volatility at the CXO Summit
content:
Exploring how CEOs Manage Volatility at the CXO Summit
Prioritise Us
As supply chains become more complex, CEOs are heading to the CXO Summit in October in order to explore leading strategies for navigating complexity
Global organisations are no longer facing isolated shocks – now, disruption has become a continuous state of business operations. CEOs are navigating global markets, with concerns about business stability and revenue growth.
This shift has pushed business leaders to
prioritise resilience
over efficiency, though many of these leaders are still failing to execute their plans effectively.
The CXO Summit, 7-8 October in London, is an opportunity for executives across all global industries to come together and discuss business strategies. Ensuring supply chains can navigate volatility is at the centre of the summit, as leaders confront a question that has moved from operations meetings into the boardroom: how do you keep a complex organisation running when markets shift without warning.
The CEO Summit, taking place on the ThinkTank Stage, brings chief executives together for open conversation on growth strategy, innovation at scale, governance and stakeholder trust, all viewed through the lens of resilience under pressure.
Attendees will hear chief executives describe what sustainable profitability looks like when supply networks face constant disruption. The panel will examine how leading CEOs weigh short-term performance against long-term transformation, and what that balance means for organisational agility across sourcing, logistics and production.
Join the CXO Summit
to gain useful insights about leading teams through turbulence.
The case for the CEO Summit's agenda rests on data that points to strain across global supply networks. According to a PwC survey of chief executives navigating global markets, only three in ten currently feel positive about revenue growth for 2026, with many struggling to convert AI investment into returns that reach the supply chain.
Approximately 12% of executives surveyed said factors such as AI have already delivered cost and revenue benefits, which could show the technology's growing role in supply chain efficiency for some global CEOs this year. Most respondents remain cautious despite this pocket of optimism.
One in five CEOs say their organisation is exposed to financial loss from tariffs, a figure that points directly at cross-border supply chain exposure. Separately, 31% cite
cyber attacks
as a major threat, a risk that extends into supplier networks and logistics systems as much as corporate infrastructure.
These pressures have pushed many CEOs towards reinvention measures aimed at protecting supply continuity as well as growth. According to the same survey, 44% of those questioned expect to invest outside their current industry, with technology named as the most attractive sector, and 51% plan to make international investments through 2026, a move that could reshape sourcing and supplier relationships across regions.
This shift suggests a growing focus on resilience among current CEOs, one where supply chain leadership sits alongside financial performance as a boardroom concern. The priority now appears to be positioning enterprises for what comes next, particularly as AI and geopolitics continue to reshape supply networks across industries.
The CEO Summit and the wider CXO Summit will give C-suite executives space to address these shared concerns over the two-day event. Attendees will also have access to branded opportunities, workshops and strategy discussion sessions built around
supply chain resilience and risk
Join the CXO Summit
On 7-8 October, the CXO Summit will be taking place place at Convene 155 Bishopsgate, London, UK, bringing together executives and speakers from global industries to explore HR, finance, marketing and supply chain strategy.
The event will unite more than 500 executives across sectors to discuss leadership strategies, network with peers and address challenges currently facing supply chains and business operations worldwide.
C-suite executives who value new perspectives and open communication will be able to hold cross-functional dialogue on capital, performance, brand and supply chain risk, across the event's dedicated CEO, CFO, CHRO and CMO zones.
The summit features talks from more than 50 industry speakers, four content zones and four executive workshops.

title: GCL SI achieves 33.44% efficiency for flexible perovskite-silicon tandem cell
content:
GCL SI achieves 33.44% efficiency for flexible perovskite-silicon tandem cell
Chinese solar module manufacturer
GCL System Integration Technology (GCL SI)
has announced a certified power conversion efficiency of 33.44% for its self-developed flexible perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell. The result was verified by the China National Center of Inspection on Solar Photovoltaic Products Quality (CPVT).
GCL SI’s flexible perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell. Image Credit: GCL SI
Developed jointly with Soochow University, the cell also achieved a device-level power-to-weight ratio exceeding 2,000 W/kg. GCL SI said its research team produced lightweight, bendable cells that resist fracture by overcoming several challenges in ultra-thin silicon substrate integration, interface passivation, and flexible stress control.
According to the company, the technology is well suited to aerospace applications, including satellites, space stations, and deep-space exploration, where the high power-to-weight ratio and mechanical flexibility of the cells are particularly valuable. The team said it is now focusing on improving long-term stability and scaling up large-area manufacturing to move the technology toward commercialization.
The new milestone can be framed alongside a similar recent flexible tandem results, achieved with Soochow University as a recurring partner across more than one program. A separate flexible tandem
developed by LONGi Green Energy together with Soochow University reached a certified 33.4%
at laboratory cell size - verified by the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) - along with 29.8% at wafer size and a power-per-weight of 1.77 W/g.
GCL previously reported
29.51% efficiency for a 2,048 cm² perovskite-silicon tandem module
, launched a
gigawatt-scale perovskite tandem module facility in Kunshan
, and, through GCL SI, helped
lead the drafting of testing standards for 3-terminal crystalline silicon-perovskite tandem cells

title: Researchers uncover the hidden chemistry driving gradual reverse-bias degradation in perovskite solar cells
content:
Researchers uncover the hidden chemistry driving gradual reverse-bias degradation in perovskite solar cells
A research team, led by Prof. Michael McGehee at the University of Colorado Boulder, working with groups at Northwestern University, the University of Arizona, the University of Washington and the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, the new name for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory), has identified the mechanism behind the slow degradation of perovskite solar cells under reverse bias — and demonstrated a fix that requires no new materials or equipment.
Reverse bias is the electrical condition that arises when part of a panel is shaded while the rest sits in full sunlight. It has long been known to damage perovskite devices, but the picture was incomplete. Current can flow under reverse bias by two routes. Where films contain large defects, electrons rush through those sites and destroy the cell outright - an acute failure mode the same group addressed in an earlier study. The second route persists even in films without such defects: current leaks through by quantum tunnelling, distributed across the whole device, degrading it gradually rather than abruptly. That slower pathway has been far harder to characterize, and existing theories could not explain why some cells degraded so quickly, or why certain architectures proved much more resilient than others.
The layers inside a solar cell form an energy landscape that charge carriers must navigate, with interfaces acting as barriers - "mountains" separating regions where electrons can sit. Under reverse bias, that barrier should be wide enough to keep carriers in place and prevent current from flowing.
Combining time-resolved electrical measurements, device modelling and materials characterization, the team found that under reverse bias the electrochemical reactions inside the cell were not merely redistributing existing charged species, as had been assumed. They were generating entirely new mobile ions. As those ions accumulate near interfaces, they progressively narrow the energy barrier until tunnelling becomes easy and damaging current can pass.
The measured effect is substantial: inferred mobile ion concentrations rose more than 100-fold, from around 1×10¹⁷ cm⁻³ to over 1×10¹⁸ cm⁻³, within just three minutes of reverse bias at −6.0 V in p-i-n perovskite diodes. The researchers attribute the increase to iodide oxidation and coupled iodine vacancy creation, which must be balanced by reduction reactions near the hole transport layer.
Rather than behaving purely as electronic components that shuttle charge, perovskite cells also operate as small chemical systems whose internal structure is reshaped by electrochemical reactions. The device physics governs ion creation, and ion creation in turn alters the device physics - a feedback loop capable of accelerating degradation well beyond what earlier models predicted.
Having identified the reactions, the team concluded the intervention point is preventing them from starting rather than repairing damage afterwards. The culprit turned out to be sub-optimal hole transport layer coverage, which allows direct contact between the transparent conducting electrode and the perovskite and facilitates the reduction reactions that generate mobile ions.
The solution required no exotic materials or new equipment - the researchers used standard materials and procedures, but ensured the HTL was deposited very smoothly to improve its coverage. With the reactions blocked, the energy landscape is preserved and the pathway to damaging current stays closed.
Taken together with the group's earlier work on abrupt, defect-driven breakdown, the new study completes a picture of both routes by which perovskite cells decompose under reverse bias - and, in each case, offers a demonstrated way to prevent it. Efficiency records tend to attract the attention, but durability under real-world conditions such as partial shading is likely to determine whether perovskite modules reach rooftops at scale.

title: How Google Is Using Wall Street Financing Techniques to Expand Chip Sales
content: Until a year or two ago, big tech firms like Google had relatively simple balance sheets, stuffed with cash that covered any debt several times over. Nowadays, thanks to massive AI spending, Google and others are adopting techniques long used on Wall Street to expand their business without taking on all the risk themselves. Google, for example, disclosed last week that it had agreed to cover as much as $44 billion worth of lease payments on data centers owned by others, if the tenant defaults. That figure, which has risen from $6.5 billion as of the end of September, reflects Google’s efforts to supply Anthropic and others with its alternative to Nvidia’s AI chips. This exposure is just one sign of how radically Alphabet’s capital structure has changed over the past year as its huge AI investments have forced it to raise money beyond its own cash. Its debt has grown to $98 billion as of June 30 from $23.6 billion a year earlier, while it issued equity for the first time in more than two decades. The reason for the fundraising became clear last week, when Alphabet reported it had burned cash—on a free cash flow basis—in the second quarter for the first time as a public company. But the $44 billion of exposure to potential defaults of data center tenants isn’t on Google’s balance sheet, although it is disclosed in the footnotes. The balance sheet shows a much smaller figure—$815 million—reflecting Google’s estimate of its likely exposure. Google has taken on these commitments—also known as backstops—as it expands its sale of AI chips known as tensor processing units. While Google rents servers powered by its TPU AI chips through Google Cloud, it is now expanding TPU use by putting them in data centers operated by other companies. These include some developed by former crypto miners, such as Hut 8 and TeraWulf, that have pivoted to running their facilities for AI. In taking on the commitments, Google is calculating that the revenue to come from TPU sales will outweigh the financial obligations of providing backstops on the leases for the data centers that will hold them, according to two people with direct knowledge of the company’s thinking. Company executives feel confident that the financial calculus pencils out well in Alphabet’s favor, one of the people said. In many of the deals, cloud startup Fluidstack is leasing and operating the planned data centers and filling them with TPU chips, then renting that capacity to Anthropic, according to people familiar with the arrangements and company disclosures. Alphabet executives look through the Fluidstack lease when they think about the backstops to consider if the end user will default on a payment or go insolvent, one of the people said. Alphabet has backstopped leases on about 2.4 gigawatts of capacity across roughly ten projects, one of the people familiar with Alphabet’s thinking said. None of those projects are yet complete, which means Alphabet’s backstops are not yet in force. The actual TPUs going in the data centers are financed separately, many via arrangements where Broadcom, which works with Google on the TPU’s design, provides a guarantee of its own. The setup means Google is essentially acting as a corporate guarantor for space to house the chips, allowing the developers to secure cheaper debt and build capacity faster than they could on their own. The figure that the company discloses in its securities filings is the maximum amount of future payments it could be on the hook for—what Google calls the notional value. A smaller figure reflects its estimate of what it is likely to pay under the guarantees. Changes in this figure, a derivatives position carried at fair value, flow through to Google’s profit and loss statement. Alphabet’s estimate of the fair value is based on its assumptions about the probability and timing of defaults and any amounts it could recover. Recent filings show how Google’s exposure has mushroomed. In October, Google said that even as the notional value was $6.5 billion, the fair value was not material. In the most recent quarter, the fair value recorded on the balance sheet was $815 million, while the notional value had ballooned to $43.8 billion. Jordan Chalfin, head of technology research at CreditSights, cautioned against getting too concerned about Alphabet’s notional numbers, at least at this point in time. “The figures that they do disclose are the max possible loss, so keep that in mind,” Chalfin said in an interview. And, he said, “there are various kinds of things that could mitigate the exposure.” Indeed, Alphabet’s disclosures say it has several options if a tenant defaults. It generally retains the right to assume the underlying lease for its own use or the use of customers, adding scarce capacity, or lease the data center space to others. Also, the company notes that many of the leases carry terms of up to 15 years, and the potential exposure declines over time. Alphabet even has the option to terminate the backstop, though two people familiar with how the termination payments can be structured said that would likely require a hefty one-time payment to compensate bond holders who relied on the backstop when they purchased the debt. The payment would effectively get converted into an ownership interest in the project, with the size of the stake based on the size of the payment and the total cost of the project, one of the people with knowledge of Alphabet’s thinking said. Not all of Alphabet’s backstop arrangements are created equally. In one transaction with Hut 8, where Google is responsible for the entirety of a 15-year lease payment if Fluidstack defaults, neither party can get out of their obligations if there’s a major construction delay, according to Fitch Ratings. That’s a contrast to deals with other developers including TeraWulf and Cipher, where there’s a termination provision for delays, Fitch said. The Hut 8 data center lease has a contract value of $7 billion, as well as another $2 billion in other expenses such as power and property tax insurance, CEO Asher Genoot said on a conference call when the deal was announced. Yet to Commence Google’s approach reflects one approach to financial engineering supporting the build-out of AI infrastructure. Its competitors have employed others. Meta, for example, has entered into joint ventures as a minority partner to build data centers in Louisiana and Texas and keep them off its balance sheet. Oracle has also relied on arrangements off the balance sheet to support its ambitions. In addition to the backstops and other guarantees, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and others have signed hundreds of billions of dollars in data center leases that have not yet begun, keeping them off the balance sheet for now. In most deals, the leases don’t officially begin until the data center is built, the chips are installed and the facility is turned on. For Alphabet, those yet-to-commence leases totaled $85.2 billion at the end of June. Another obligation, financial guarantees that act as backstops allowing its partners to secure power and energy equipment, totaled an additional $7.6 billion. And more backstops are coming that Alphabet will likely have to account for. It said it has agreed to provide another $24.1 billion of future backstops to support data center and energy assets, subject to the finalization of terms. Google’s business remains strong, to be sure. The company generated more than $185 billion in operating cash flow over the past 12 months, and despite its recent stock and bond sales, it still has a robust ability to raise more funding. If the worst were to happen, Alphabet could also dial back on spending. Anubhav Arora, a credit analyst at Fitch Ratings, underlined the importance of that financial strength when the firm rates debt related to the data center deals. He explained that Fitch relies “very heavily on the backstop that Google has provided” to assign the projects an investable rating. He doesn’t anticipate Google’s activity slowing down anytime soon. “We continue to see more deals with Google backstops for unrated tenants, so I clearly expect the trend to continue,” he said. Sharing in the Upside At the same time, Google has structured many of its deals so it stands to collect some of the upside if the data center developers’ shares perform well. In some cases, but not all, the company has collected equity warrants in return for its backstop. It holds warrants, for example, that would allow it to own 14% of TeraWulf, which is building a data center for Fluidstack in Barker, N.Y. Google also has warrants potentially worth 5.4% of Cipher Digital, which is building a data center in Colorado City, Texas, in a similar arrangement. There’s one notable exception so far. When Hut 8 announced its own deal with Fluidstack and Anthropic in December, the company didn’t give up warrants in return for Google’s backstop. That deal, one of the people with knowledge of Alphabet’s thinking said, was an anomaly and isn’t likely to be repeated.
